### Problem: Build Array from Permutation {#sec-arr-p4-b}

::: {.p-statement}
Given a zero-based **permutation** `nums` ($1 \le n \le 1000$, $0 \le \text{nums}[i] < n$, all distinct), build `ans` with $\text{ans}[i] = \text{nums}[\text{nums}[i]]$ for every $i$. Example: $[0, 2, 1, 5, 3, 4] \to [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 3]$. Follow-up: use $O(1)$ extra memory.

Source: [LC 1920 · Build Array from Permutation](https://leetcode.com/problems/build-array-from-permutation/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Every value of a permutation is a valid index, so `nums[nums[i]]` is always in range: read a value, use it as an index, read again. For the in-place follow-up, store the answer in the high "digit" of each cell, `old + n * new`, so the old value stays readable as `cell % n`.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Allocate the answer.** Fill a fresh array with `ans[i] = nums[nums[i]]`: $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ extra space. The cell `nums[nums[i]]` must keep its original value until every reader has used it, which is why writing the answer straight into `nums` fails.
2. **Encode two values in every cell.** Write the answer into the same array as a second digit in base $n$ (@eq-arr-encode): `nums[i] += n * (nums[nums[i]] % n)`. Cell $i$ itself is still original when step $i$ runs (we process left to right, and only cell $i$ changes at step $i$), but its source `nums[nums[i]]` may already carry an answer, so it is read through `% n`. A second pass divides every cell by $n$.

**Invariant.** Before step $i$, every cell $j < i$ holds $\text{old}_j + n\cdot\text{ans}_j$ and every cell $j \ge i$ holds $\text{old}_j$; in both cases $\text{cell}_j \bmod n = \text{old}_j$, so any original value can still be read.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Allocate an answer and double-index

::: {.form-next}
Read the definition literally into a new array. Because `nums` is a permutation, `nums[i]` is always a valid index. $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ extra space for the answer.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def build_brute(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    return [nums[nums[i]] for i in range(len(nums))]
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<int> buildArray(vector<int>& nums) {
    vector<int> ans(nums.size());
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)nums.size(); ++i)
        ans[i] = nums[nums[i]];
    return ans;
}
```
:::

#### Encode two values in every cell

::: {.form-next}
Keep the same double lookup but write the answer into the cell itself, as the high digit of a base-$n$ pair: `nums[i] += n * (nums[nums[i]] % n)`, then `nums[i] //= n` for every cell. The `% n` on the inner read is what recovers an original value that already carries an answer. $O(1)$ extra space; the cells reach at most $n^2 - 1 < 10^6$, comfortably inside an `int`.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("build", "encode")
    assert str(final) == "[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 3]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-build-perm
def build_inplace(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    a, n = nums, len(nums)
    for i in range(n):
        a[i] += n * (a[a[i]] % n)       # a[i] is still original; its source may be encoded
    for i in range(n):
        a[i] //= n                      # keep only the new value
    return a


def build_no_mod(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:     # the bug: reads an encoded cell raw
    a, n = nums, len(nums)
    for i in range(n):
        a[i] += n * a[a[i]]
    return [x // n for x in a]


for _ in range(2000):
    n = random.randint(1, 10)
    a = random.sample(range(n), n)      # a true permutation
    assert build_inplace(list(a)) == build_brute(a)

assert build_inplace([0, 2, 1, 5, 3, 4]) == [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 3]    # the board sample
assert build_inplace([5, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4]) == [4, 5, 0, 1, 2, 3]
assert build_no_mod([1, 2, 0]) == [2, 0, 7] != build_brute([1, 2, 0]) == [2, 0, 1]   # without % n
print("build OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<int> buildArrayInplace(vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        nums[i] += n * (nums[nums[i]] % n);   // answer in the high digit; n*n <= 10^6 fits in int
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        nums[i] /= n;                          // read the answer back
    return nums;
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Allocate an answer and double-index** is $O(n)$ time, one double lookup per index, and $O(n)$ extra space for `ans`. **Encode two values in every cell** keeps $O(n)$ time (two passes) and needs $O(1)$ extra space. The encoded values stay below $n^2 \le 10^6$ here; for $n$ above about $46\,000$ they would need `long long` (@sec-arr-cost).
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Identity permutation: `ans == nums`.
- A cycle like $[1, 2, 0]$: the answer is $[2, 0, 1]$. Without `% n` on the inner read, step $2$ reads cell $0$ after it became $1 + 3\cdot2 = 7$, and the last answer comes out as $7$ instead of $1$; `build_no_mod` shows it.
- $n = 1$: $[0] \to [0]$; every cell is $0 + 1\cdot0$.
:::
